messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Frank Miller was 71 years old, a North American man who had spent most of his adult life working in security, a role he had taken seriously as both an occupation and a duty. Married now for many years, he had always thought of himself as someone who stayed calm under pressure and could look after others by keeping watch. That sense of himself changed after the terrorist attack that occurred during one of his shifts. He had been on duty in a public building when the violence broke out suddenly and without warning, turning an ordinary work setting into a scene of panic, shouting, and immediate danger. In the days that followed, Frank found that he could remember the frightening event in unusually sharp detail: particular sounds, the look on people’s faces, the sequence of moments as they unfolded. At the same time, he was distressed by how uneven those memories felt. At times he could recall what happened with cold precision, as if he were replaying a recording, yet feel strangely numb, as though it had happened to somebody else. He also struggled to make sense of it as a single story. Even when he tried to tell his wife or think through it alone, the account would not come together cleanly in his mind, leaving him with fragments rather than a clear beginning, middle, and end.

As the weeks passed, Frank began to live as if danger could appear anywhere. He became vigilant for dangerous people whenever he was in public, scanning faces and movements automatically, especially in places that felt crowded or unfamiliar. At work, this took on a practical shape: he would choose positions that let him see who was entering and leaving, and he always sat with his back against a wall so he could keep the room in view. What had once been a preference became an absolute habit, followed without much thought but with real urgency. He told himself that if he could not see everyone, he could not trust the situation. In his mind, the attack had shown that danger could arrive in an instant, and he was determined not to be caught unprepared again. Even ordinary outings with his wife became more effortful because he was constantly checking the people around him rather than settling into the moment. He found himself watching for the kind of person he believed could do something terrible, and that watchfulness stayed with him in stores, restaurants, and waiting rooms.

Frank also found himself returning over and over to thoughts of revenge. He ruminated about how to get even with the assailant, turning the idea around in his mind in long, repetitive stretches. The thoughts did not bring relief so much as keep the event present, as though he were still in a state of unfinished business with the person responsible. He did not speak much about these thoughts, but they left him preoccupied and tense. He had come to believe that someone else would not have gotten into this situation, that another man might have done better, reacted faster, or somehow prevented it. That comparison sat heavily on him because security had been the role in life that gave him pride. Now he felt he had failed in that most important role. The sense of failure was not abstract; it was tied to his identity as someone who was supposed to notice danger before others did and keep people safe. Instead, he was left feeling that he could not deal with even the slightest upset, let alone something as overwhelming as what had happened that day.

Over time, these experiences shaped how Frank moved through daily life with his wife and in his job. He remained working, but the job no longer felt straightforward or secure in the way it once had. He was more guarded around people, and the need to position himself carefully in rooms made him appear distant and watchful. His wife noticed that he was harder to settle and more consumed by his own vigilance. Frank himself felt increasingly worn down by the effort it took to keep himself composed. He finally sought help because the memories remained vivid, the numbness was unsettling, and the sense of failure had become hard to carry. What frightened him most was the feeling that he might never regain confidence in his own judgment or his ability to protect himself and others. What he hoped for, if anything could help, was some way to live without constantly bracing for the next threat and without the burden of believing he had fallen short in the role that had defined him.
